nutshell: Standard person ReID models trained only to match identities still encode enough personally identifiable information (PII) in their features to let an attacker re-identify individuals or reconstruct images. PEPR-Net addresses this with two stages: (1) training-time suppression via a self-supervised de-identification decoder plus an adversarial-identity module, and (2) an optional deployment-time controllable-privacy mechanism that applies differential-privacy Gaussian noise to gallery features with a user-tunable privacy budget.
contributions: A privacy metric for ReID: quantifying PII leakage as the accuracy with which a held-out identity classifier can re-identify individuals from the learned ReID features (lower ID accuracy = better privacy), used consistently to evaluate both the proposed method and prior work that never reported this.

Stage 1 (training-time): a De-ID decoder that reconstructs pixelated (de-identified) versions of the input from ReID features, plus an adversarial-identity module that pushes the softmax identity-prediction distribution toward uniform - both trained jointly with the standard ReID triplet loss via a weighted multi-task objective.

Stage 2 (deployment-time): a controllable (epsilon, delta)-differential-privacy mechanism that adds Gaussian noise directly to gallery embeddings after training, letting an operator dial privacy up or down post-hoc via a single budget parameter without retraining the model.

Empirically shows the two stages are complementary: applying the same DP noise to baseline (undefended) features only modestly reduces identity leakage, while applying it on top of the Stage-1 privacy-preserving features achieves a much larger leakage reduction at comparable utility cost.

Outperforms several existing privacy-preserving ReID baselines (DP-SGD, federated-learning variants, face-blurring methods, PIS) on ReID utility (mAP/Top-1) while being one of the only methods among them to actually report a quantified privacy-leakage number.
deficiencies: The privacy metric only tests one specific attack: whether a held-out softmax/linear classifier can predict identity from the features. The paper's own Figure 1 motivates the work partly with a decoder-reconstruction attack threat, and Figure 7 shows qualitative reconstructed images, but no quantitative reconstruction-attack success metric is reported against the final trained model - the headline privacy number covers identity-inference risk only, not the reconstruction risk it also motivates.

The paper's own Table 1 ablation shows the Adversarial-Identity (Adv-ID) module alone is the single most damaging component to utility (Market-1501 mAP drops from 69.22 to 55.90, worse than any De-ID variant alone), yet it is retained in the final model at a small loss weight without questioning whether its privacy benefit independently justifies its utility cost versus, say, using only the De-ID decoder.

The SOTA comparison (Tables 3-4) is not symmetric: several compared privacy-preserving baselines (DP-SGD, Federated-by-Camera, face-blur variants) report no privacy/ID-leakage numbers at all (shown as '-'), so the claim of 'achieving a better trade-off between Re-ID performance and privacy' than these methods can only actually be verified on the utility axis for those rows, not the privacy axis that is the paper's central contribution.

Differential privacy is applied only to gallery features at test time using an empirically chosen noise range (dataset standard deviation +/- 5) rather than a principled per-dataset sensitivity derivation, and Stage 1's privacy improvement (De-ID + Adv-ID) carries no formal privacy guarantee - only Stage 2 has an actual (epsilon, delta)-DP proof, so the combined system's overall privacy guarantee is partial rather than end-to-end.
notable: Table 2 shows a genuinely useful synergy finding: at matched privacy budget (epsilon=0.5), adding DP noise to baseline features only drops identity-leakage accuracy by 12.34 points, but adding the identical DP mechanism on top of the Stage-1 privacy-preserving features drops it by 50.44 points at a comparable utility cost - evidence that layering a training-time defense with a deployment-time one is meaningfully more effective than either alone, useful for anyone designing similar layered privacy pipelines. Also notable: the ablation directly compares blurring, obfuscation, and pixelation as the De-ID decoder's reconstruction target and finds pixelation clearly best for utility-privacy trade-off (Table 1) - a concrete, transferable design choice.
